items.content:
If you've spent a considerable amount of time surfing the internet (and especially the Small Web), you might have seen an 88x31 button, or a few dozen of them. Some of them look like this:

However, the nice thing about computer displays is that they are able to cope with quickly changing visuals, hence some have animation:

I have noticed that among very numerous examples , i haven't seen any that'd go very far in that axis. Usually the animations are there just to catch your eye, or to display several words in succession. But why not Moby Dick?

I was surprised to find that there seems to be no limit to the number of frames in a GIF file, and that the maximum resolution is 2^16 by 2^16, which is 4295 megapixels. We are of course limiting ourselves to just 88 by 31 pixels (or 0.003 megapixel), which might mean that regular text fonts don't get much space to shine — Arial, for example, seems to become legible at a minimum of 10 pixels height, which allows us to display about eleven words at once.

As is often the case in computing, popular conventions end up upsetting someone enough that they develop an alternative way. In this case the alternative we're looking for are fonts designed to be legible at extremely low font sizes. There are some as small as 3x3, but personally I find TomThumb to be the golden middle here. You can get TomThumb in truetype here .

Firstly, you will want to obtain a plain text copy of the book's content. The methods might vary depending on what formats you have access to — you can use OCR to grab the text from a physical book , with an .EPUB or .PDF you can convert them (or even copy text manually), or you might get lucky and find what you're looking already shipped as a plain text .txt file, as is the case with Moby Dick .

I downloaded the file and stripped the license at the start and the end. I also cropped off everything before the first chapter.

If we take our button, which is 88x31, and our font, which is 6x4 (5x3 + spacing), we find that we can fit 5 rows of 22 characters each. ImageMagick, the tool we're going to use, is not very good at laying out text, so it'd be wise to take care of that ourselves. There's several ways to do this, but the neatest one uses three posix tools: cat, tr and fold:

cat is used to send the text to tr. tr translates each newline into a space, condensing the whole text file into one line. fold then takes that one line, splits it into multiple lines that are up to 22 characters wide (-w 22), and tries to avoid splitting words in half (-s).

It's likely that at this point, your text looks fine. Mine was a bit garbled up, because fold doesn't handle multibyte characters well. I checked what non-ascii characters input.txt contained, and got rid of them using sed, like this: sed -i 's/”/"/g' . The -i flag allows you to modify the file in place. You can find all the non-ascii characters using grep: grep -P -n '[^\x00-\x7F]' input.txt .

Of course, formatting is subjective. Depending on the kind of literary work, you might want to do it differently. I used sed -i 's/CHAPTER /\n\n\nCHAPTER /g' input.txt to add some space between chapters, but chapters may be marked differently in the text you're using, or they might not be present at all.

For this part, you're going to need ImageMagick installed. Although it's likely that you already have it. We use the following command to generate the first version of our GIF file:

Note that I have the actual tom.ttf file placed in the current working directory. It's mostly self explanatory. Convert takes the text from standard input and, just like that, puts it onto a GIF, frame by frame. Lovely. However, it seems to force some margin on the bottom of the image, which is why we drew the text on an image eight pixiels higher than we wanted. We're going to crop it now:

items.title: OpenAI models hacked a crypto wallet and breached more websites
items.content:
OpenAI said internal models hacked two more websites, bypassed company-imposed browsing restrictions, and used exposed credentials to draw cryptocurrency from a wallet it couldn’t otherwise access, in the latest installment of disclosures of its agents performing unethical and likely illegal acts.

The company on Thursday issued reports of four new incidents, all of which occurred in June. They come after the company revealed in July that internal test agents exploited a zero-day vulnerability in a tool designed to restrict their access to the Internet. They then broke into the network of AI tool provider Hugging Face. The agents took that illegal action to steal answers to a hacking test that weren’t available when completing the tasks on their own. The incident—which likely would have resulted in criminal charges had they been performed directly by a person—has further heightened concerns that widespread AI use could have harmful effects on an unprecedented scale.

Easier to beg for forgiveness than ask permission

In two of the cases reported Thursday, OpenAI agents tasked with retrieving information from websites hacked them when the models ran into obstacles obtaining it directly. In one incident during reinforcement training, a model that received access denials when trying to retrieve historical hospital-bed statistics on a government statistics website “used the site’s file-download feature to retrieve server configuration and application files, including sensitive credentials,” OpenAI said . “It inspected the application code, bypassed the statistics endpoint’s authorization checks, and retrieved data that had previously been denied. The model saved the data locally.”

In the other incident , a model instructed to retrieve figures from a public research dashboard bypassed the organization’s security controls and used the unauthorized access to steal credentials. It then made configuration changes on the server.

In one evaluation, the changes let the model make an internal search tool relay queries to the public dashboard. In a second evaluation, the model downloaded five non-public tables containing 147,451 rows. OpenAI researchers had prompted the agents to retrieve only five dashboard figures. Even after resetting the setting, the model continued using the token to retrieve non-public data.

items.title: CTRL+SHIFT+T: a new page for the Tech Workers Movement
items.content:
People have seen empires come and go. These times are not special. When an empire crumbles, the political game splits between accelerating the process, protecting the most vulnerable from the falling debris, and starting to plan for what comes next.

New formations revolving around technology redefine the contour of the political arena: Effective Altruism, Accelerationists, Neo-Luddites, Doomsday cults, AI worshippers, Tech Monarchists, Hardline Primitivists.

I’ve just finished reading “All In: A Revolutionary Theory to Stop Climate Collapse,” and I’ve been positively surprised by its ambition. The book frames a specific approach to strategy development for the environmental movement, then generalizes it to a strategy to rupture the entire political system. It starts from the premise that science sets a very clear deadline, a few years from now, before irreversible catastrophic chain reactions will jeopardize the survival of the majority of the human population. The target outcome is the establishment of a different path in which emissions reach 0 by around 2030. The main strategic frame passes through disarming capitalism in the span of a few years. From this, follow several strategic conclusions which I won’t recapitulate here.

The book tries to be as critical as possible towards the existing strategies and organizations of the environmental movement, including the ones the authors supported. This is done to push forward a plurality of approaches, rather than proposing a single, unitary new strategy. Such an approach, called occasionally “movement ecology”, is complemented with an organizational materialist perspective, i.e. the idea that the transformation of the material and social world is driven primarily by the development of organizational capacities. Politics as a conflict of organized forces rather than a conflict of ideas.

I think it’s easy to appreciate the bold proposition behind the “movement intervention” the book represents, and the attempt at condensing into specific, actionable recommendations for the environmental movement what is the new “organizational common sense” built on systems theory, Nunes’ political ecology digested through Ulex ’s educational program, and the lived practice of organizational experimentation that sets environmentalists apart from most other political spaces, at least in Europe.

Now, if “All In” doesn’t sound ambitious enough, in this piece, I will try to repeat the same exercise for the Western Tech Workers Movement, in a single paper. It is still an “intervention from within”, even though, given the differences between the current state of the environmental movement and the Tech Workers Movement, mine will be less dramatic and more focused on expanding the horizon of what has to be tried.

Let’s narrow down the scope of our exercise:

– Targets of coordination: the western Tech Workers Movement, understood as that portion of the labor movement aware of the necessity of organizing tech workers according to their own specificities. This means labor organizations such as unions, union confederations, workers’ collectives and communities, cooperatives, and labor NGOs active within or around tech companies. The focus of the article is on the USA and European context, the one I know the best, but not necessarily restricted to it.

– Winning condition:  tech labor becoming a primary force pushing for Democratic Control of Technology (DeCoTech), understood as the historical project of wrestling technological production, maintenance, and governance away from Capital to be put in control and service of new democratic counter-institutions. It is understood as a general political direction to pick provisional and context-specific, rather than fixed and universal, goals. items.title: JPEG XL vs. AVIF for web use-cases
items.content:
JPEG XL has now landed in all major browsers, so I figured I'd take a closer look at what it's good/bad at compared to other formats.

I'll go into full detail, with examples and benchmarks, but for those of you who don't have the time, here are the headlines:

For lossy photos on the web, AVIF almost always produces smaller files than JPEG XL. At default effort settings, the best JPEG XL version is typically 15–25% larger than the equivalent AVIF. At maximum effort settings, the gap narrows a little, to typically 6–20%. There are outliers, where JPEG XL is close to, or even beats AVIF, so if you want the absolute best result for a particular image, it's worth trying both. See the F1 image for a typical example, and the weasel for an outlier.

The JPEG XL encoder matters a lot. jixel , a newer JPEG XL encoder, usually produces smaller files than libjxl , except when the image has detailed transparency. The people image is one example.

For screenshots and illustrations, AVIF is much better than JPEG XL. The equivalent JPEG XL is 30–90% larger at default effort settings, and 20–70% larger at maximum effort settings. Lossy AVIF handles these well - you don't need to use lossless formats unless you really need bit-exact results. See the screenshot and illustration examples.

For images with transparency, AVIF is much better than JPEG XL. The libjxl version is 31–44% larger at default effort settings, and 61–70% larger at maximum effort settings. jixel always encodes transparency losslessly, which makes its files 2–3x the size of AVIF's. See the data .

AVIF is generally faster to encode, and uses less memory, when you factor in file size. jixel is faster than AVIF and uses less memory, but its files are typically significantly larger, so AVIF is better on balance. See the F1 image for one example.

AVIF is faster to decode. JPEG XL typically takes 2–3x as long to decode at medium quality, but the gap narrows at very high qualities, where Chrome can sometimes decode JPEG XL faster. The people image is one example.

Higher effort settings are worth it for AVIF and jixel, but not libjxl. libjxl's higher efforts are much slower, use a lot more memory, and barely improve the result. Sometimes they produce larger files than the default effort. The screenshot is an example of this.

AVIF's 4:2:0 mode (half colour resolution) shouldn't be your default. It rarely reduces file size, and it makes higher qualities harder to reach. Although, it is quicker to encode and decode. Stick with 4:4:4 if you don't have time to check both. The F1 image is one example, and the screenshot is an exception.

Quality settings are reliable for all the encoders. With a single quality setting, the resulting quality varies a bit between images, but all the encoders vary in the same direction, and in ways that seem reasonable. See the data .

Progressive JPEG XL is basically free at high effort. jixel recently added support for early progressive previews, and at its slowest setting they cost little or nothing, but at its default setting the files are 12% bigger. Firefox and Chrome support progressive JPEG XL. Safari still renders the final image, but doesn't show progressive previews. However, is this type of progressive rendering a good user experience? See the examples and data .

AVIF supports progressive rendering! It's Chrome-only for now, but it's in progress for Firefox. It's more complex than progressive JPEG XL, but it gives you more control over what the preview looks like, the files are usually smaller, and they're much faster to decode. See for yourself .

For HDR, JPEG XL lacks gain maps, which is a significant limitation compared to AVIF. The JPEG XL format supports gain maps, but they aren't supported by browser decoders, and the encoding story is messy/experimental. When comparing non-gain mapped HDR content, the two quality metrics I used disagree a lot, but they agree that JPEG XL produces smaller files compared to AVIF. See the examples…

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

items.title: MapQuest will now show you where Flock cameras are in your neighborhood
items.content:
MapQuest will now show you where Flock cameras are in your neighborhood

You can see the locations of known outdoor surveillance cameras in the app.

MapQuest has been on quite the unexpected tear over the last couple of months. The mapping service's app surged in popularity after it refused to refer to Lake Ontario as Lake America (unlike Google Maps and Apple Maps ). MapQuest also added useful, long-overdue features like Android Auto support and public transit directions .

The app now has another handy tool . You can toggle a layer that shows known outdoor surveillance cameras and license plate readers.

The layer will show you where  Flock cameras  are. It also displays the locations of cameras from the likes of Motorola Solutions (Vigilant), Genetec, Axis Communications, Axon, Leonardo (ELSAG), Neology, Rekor, PlateSmart, Ubicquia and Verkada. The layer sits alongside options to view traffic and incidents, so it should be easy to find in the app.

MapQuest announced the update with a short video that's set to Rockwell's "Somebody's Watching Me." Chef's kiss, no notes.

You might not be able to easily avoid these cameras on your commute or other usual routes, but the layer may be helpful in illustrating how pervasive these things are in your area. It's useful information to have for those who are trying to rid their neighborhoods of surveillance cams.

For many years, Codeberg Pages v2, our in-house solution, served as a way for hosting project pages through your_codeberg_username .codeberg.page or custom domains. This project has been unmaintained for a longer time now, and we already have git-pages as a replacement to power Codeberg Pages. A lot of users already migrated - and now it is time for you to also make the switch, if you have not done already.

On that date, for users who are still relying on the old way of hosting sites through Codeberg Pages v2 (which is the case for users who never set up a webhook in their repository), the content will not be served anymore.

We already have instructions how to do so. So please refer to our Migration Guide for migrating.

If you do not remember whether you migrated or not, you can test yourself by using our Migration Check Tool . Just paste an URL and get a definite answer.

items.title: In Europe’s tech capital, Irish labor unions are booming amid AI-driven layoffs
items.content:
DUBLIN — The Irish capital, which doubles as Europe's de facto tech capital, hosted two very different AI summits in the past week.

Most eyes were on the International AI Summit , the signature tech event of Ireland's six-month presidency of the Council of the EU, where top brass from the world's biggest tech firms discussed ways to harness artificial intelligence and minimize safety risks.

But the weekend before, a very different conversation was taking place at the Workers' AI Counter Summit , as Ireland's tech workers demanded a say in how the burgeoning technology reshapes the workplace and society.

Ireland's lucrative tech sector has been rattled by waves of AI-driven layoffs — and the country's fledgling tech union has seen an exponential spike in sign-ups from workers who are worried about their future.

There’s an “awakening” happening right now among workers in Ireland’s tech sector, and a growing “awareness that they’re not bulletproof,” said Sinéad Gibney, a social democrat lawmaker who previously worked for Google.

“I do think what we will see is that parts of roles will be automated, which means that people will be competing more heavily for the same roles," she said. "They won't have the same labor power and therefore we're going to see a drop in quality of work, we're going to see more zero-hour contracts, in more places than we already see it.”

The labor movement brewing in Ireland, where many of the world's tech giants have their EU bases, is part of a wider trend among tech workers globally, who have seen their work disrupted by rapidly evolving AI.

Ireland’s dedicated union for tech workers, the Digital and Techworker Alliance (DATA), has seen a five-fold increase in membership since it was first founded in 2023.

In its first year and a half of existence, membership hovered around 270 people. In the past year-and-a-half, it's jumped to more than 1,350 members, DATA organizer John Bohan told POLITICO.  He added that this number tends to spike around layoffs and other actions.

“The tech industry was founded on the idea that it would never have a union, because they're making people rich, and treat them really well,” Bohan said.  “But post-Covid, workforce adjustments happened again and again, with layoffs and declining conditions in the sector. We started to see more people wanting to get organized around redundancies.”

The spike in sign-ups coincides with a wave of layoffs in Ireland’s tech bubble (and the tech sector globally ), as companies corrected pandemic-era overhiring, and diverted investment to AI.

Ireland hosts the EU headquarters of most of the world’s largest tech companies, and more than 170,000 people are employed in the tech sector, according to the country's statistics institute.

Social media giant Meta has roughly halved its workforce in Ireland since the pandemic, axing well over 1,000 roles to offset AI investment and boost efficiency. Separately, Meta subcontractor Covalen also announced massive layoffs earlier this year, cutting more than 700 people.

Video-sharing platform TikTok announced this year it would shed around 300 Irish jobs , mostly from its trust and safety team, shifting the work to other countries, outsourced vendors or automated AI solutions.

A report by the IMF earlier this year warned that Ireland’s labor market is “relatively more exposed” to AI than many advanced economies, partly due to its concentration of tech workers.

The AI race is also creating new jobs on the Irish market – as AI firms like Anthropic and OpenAI are setting up Irish bases and trying to lure Big Tech workers with even bigger salaries.

Amid the uncertainty and volatility of the AI boom, tech workers are turning to unions for the first time as a safety net. One tech worker who used to work in trust and safety at a big tech firm told POLITICO that there used to be a feeling that as a “pampered” tech worker you “can't ask for your rights, because you already have it so much…

Big Fish: Exploiting a 37-Year-Old Kernel Bug in OpenBSD
items.summary: openbsd, security
items.content:
Big Fish: Exploiting a 37-Year-Old Kernel Bug in OpenBSD

Calif frequently publishes our offensive research and work, but we otherwise don't draw much attention to the defensive work we do — assisting open source projects with remediation, patch generation, cryptographic improvements, and internal engineering projects we carry out for our clients.

Earlier this year, we reported some vulnerabilities, often along with suggested patches to OpenBSD. One traced back roughly 37 years to the original BSD sources , where a shared memory attachment counter was defined as a signed 16-bit short. Repeatedly forking a process with shared memory attachment records could push that counter past its maximum value of 32,767, causing it to wrap to a negative value. This integer overflow could lead to a use-after-free via a race condition; combined with a separate out-of-bounds write in the kernel, it allowed local privilege escalation to root. The issues were addressed in errata 026 and 018 , respectively.

We managed to get local root in OpenBSD with KARL / SMAP / SMEP enabled without the use of an information disclosure vulnerability via the following path:

Map 127 SysV shared memory segments, unmap them via munmap() , and fork 259 processes to wrap the shared memory attach count to -32,643. Perform heap grooming and layout, using metrics from sysctl( KERN_MALLOCSTATS) (such as kb_total and kb_totalfree ) to track allocations and determine when new pages are allocated. Win the race condition using IPC_RMID in one process while attaching a new size-confused shared memory segment in a helper process. Align IP socket allocations and set IP_MULTICAST_TTL to a non-default value of 2 to allocate a persistent 16-byte struct ip_moptions . Its final word packs two 16-bit counters: imo + 12 = imo_num_memberships | imo_max_memberships << 16 . Trigger the conditional -1 out-of-bounds write to overwrite both the number of memberships and maximum memberships fields. close() the socket to traverse the group members, triggering atomic decrements that modify the PTE self-referential mapping twice, switching it from user to supervisor accessible mapping, and achieving kernel code execution by overwriting a predictable kernel pointer. Clean up shared memory accounting and restore the overwritten kernel pointer to obtain a root shell.

That's the short of the matter , the longer version is more interesting , including the history of the vulnerability, as a short shm_nattch can be traced back ~37 years ago , in the original BSD sources.

Taking a step back, this vulnerability ended up getting code execution via a write what where primitive, where the write was caused by a TAILQ_REMOVE , the what was our userland memory mapping that was made supervisor mode accessible to bypass SMAP / SMEP , and the where was a predictable kernel pointer location.

While OpenBSD's KARL relinks the kernel binary to randomize both function and data addresses, the kernel's memory allocators remain deterministic. Both the boot-time allocator and the best-fit allocator lack base address randomization. Consequently, early boot allocations consistently land at predictable locations across boots on the same hardware. When these predictable structure allocations contain function pointers, they become ideal targets for exploitation. For instance, the exploit reliably targets the lo0 and enc0 ioctl handlers, overwriting one to gain control flow and using the other to restore the overwritten pointer.

Aside from the aforementioned errata fixes, there's several other approaches that can be taken to either eliminate or reduce the likelihood of those avenues being used again.

Firstly, we can implement safe-unlinking, a technique that checks doubly linked list invariants before performing the unlink memory writes. If the invariants are violated, then a suitable abort() or panic() is called, depending on if user mode or kernel mode, preventing memory corruption from occurring. An example…

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.title: Valve’s Steam Client for Linux Goes 64-bit in Beta and Moves Into a Container
items.content:
Valve's October 15 Steam Client Beta changes how the Linux client is built and run. It moves the client to a 64-bit build and runs it inside a Steam Runtime container. Alongside that, a fix for the updater window failing to show up is included, as is the new Achievement Sets feature.

According to Valve, the client has run in an older setup that layers Steam Runtime libraries over the ones on the host system. The runtime documentation adds that this only works while the host is newer than the runtime.

Games on Steam can already run in containers, which give an application its own set of libraries rather than blending them with the host's. The tool behind those containers, pressure-vessel , still takes graphics drivers from the host system.

Valve says running the client in a container should make it behave more consistently across distros . Its games already run on the same technology.

The release notes for the beta client do not name the container, but its runtime release notes tie the 64-bit client to one called steamrt3c . The README describes it as a variant of the sniper runtime made for use inside the Steam client.

The groundwork for this can be traced back to March, when Valve put the container and the early 64-bit client out as the Linux SteamRT3 Beta .

And don't assume that opting for a 64-bit client removes the need for 32-bit libraries .

The requirements for the beta client still call for both 32-bit and 64-bit versions of the required libraries and graphics drivers on x86_64 systems.

They also list 64-bit-only setups as unsupported . The steamrt3c README from earlier notes that its containers ship i386 libraries for compatibility with older software.

I switched to the beta on Ubuntu 26.04 LTS, and it only took me four steps. If Steam is not already on your system, you need to get the official DEB package for the client and install it.

Open Steam, click Steam at the top left, and choose Settings .

Go into the Interface tab and find Client Beta Participation .

Open the dropdown and select Steam Beta Update .

Click Restart Now when Steam asks you to restart.

That is all it takes, and Steam is now on the beta channel. Valve welcomes bug reports from testers, so if you run into an issue, use the " Report a bug " button in the Interface page.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.
